selected_candidates.caption:
When you’re dealing with a complex gut health issue, one perspective often isn’t enough. True healing happens when we stop looking at the gut in one symptom or issue at a time and start looking at the whole person. This takes a multidisciplinary approach. 

In a collaborative care model, your team works like a well-oiled machine. Here is how each “player” on your team brings something unique to the table:

The Gastroenterologist: The coach of the team. They’re looking into the internal issues, calling the plays. This may be using scopes and imaging to identify structural issues, inflammation, or disease. 🧑‍⚕️ 🩺 

Advanced Practice Provider (NP or PA): The quarterback, running plays. We dive deep into the clinical management, symptom tracking, and the long-term plan, ensuring your treatment fits into your actual life. Continue to monitor and tweak therapies to help manage your care. Nurse 👩🏻‍⚕️ 

The GI Dietitian: The special teams. They move beyond “avoidance” to help you find a sustainable way to eat that nourishes your body without triggering a flare. 🍎

The GI Psychologist: The offense or the brain-gut specialist. They help manage the literal “nervous system” of the gut, addressing how stress and the brain-gut axis impact your physical symptoms. 🧠

The patient: Team owner. The one who has final say, and has input on how the team is working together to deliver results.

When we communicate and collaborate, you get better results, faster.

Does your current care plan include a multidisciplinary team? Tell us how your specialists have made a difference in your journey below! 👇

visible_text.text: What are the roles of your GI team

spoken_content.text: GI care
shouldn't be just one person.
It's a whole team.
Let's meet them and what they do.
Hi, I'm a registered
dietitian, and registered dietitians help GI patients
navigate what they can and cannot eat.
Usually, we would like patients to see us as soon as they're recommended an elimination diet or any diet to trial.
However, a lot of the times, we see patients when they come in, they're already very afraid of food.
So if you are a GI patient, go see a registered dietitian to help you figure out a diet that works for you, doesn't trigger symptoms, and minimum limitations.
The role of GI psychologist is very important because we help patients understand the connection between your brain and your gut.

And then we offer evidence-based brain gut behavioral therapies that really target things like motility, your abdominal pain, as well as improving your coping and resilience around the management of these conditions.
When I see GI patients,
I'm there to get the history, do a physical.
Then I help diagnose.
Um, then I will refer to a physician to do an endoscopy or colonoscopy.
And often times I will continue to follow and manage them through their clinical course.
To provide patient education, medications,
and other treatment modalities.
Gastroenterologist takes the lead with diagnosis, um, performing any endoscopies and colonoscopies and then ordering the diagnostic testing.
Right. So in addition to that, we have the treatments available as well, which are often dependent on what the endoscopic evaluation is, but also more in terms of just medical therapies as well.

And then I think, um, the gastroenterologist helps also take the lead in coordinating the rest of the healthcare team. Um, you're often the first person or we're often the first person that you see and then we can help connect you with any appropriate referrals with a dietitian, a psychologist, um, working with any of our APPs, um, for a follow-up treatment as well.
Additionally, we're also care coordinators because often times
we're the first people who are diagnosed with colon cancer, so we are referring to oncologists, talking to the primary care physician, uh, surgeons,
um, and then in terms of metabolic things also endocrinologist as well.
So, uh, we are both, you know, physicians, but we also coordinate care for all of our patients.

EAST TO DIGEST FIBER RICH FOODS

FOODS THAT HEAL YOUR GUT

spoken_content.text: Here's a list of foods I would start eating every day if I was trying to heal my gut.
These foods specifically have gut healing properties and I'm going to break down each one for you and explain why they help.
Get used to eating these things on a regular basis and watch bloating and constipation disappear.
Let's start with our enzyme rich foods.
So enzymes are little proteins that help you to break down and digest food.
When you increase enzyme rich foods in your diet, you help your gut digest better. It'll stop bloating before it even happens.
My favorite enzyme rich foods to tell people to include are kiwis, papayas and pineapple.
There's actually a lot of research on two kiwis a day being one of the most helpful things that you can do to heal IBS.
Now we're moving on to probiotic rich foods.
And probiotic rich foods can also be high in enzymes, like sauerkraut, kimchi or kefir.
Only need about a tablespoon of these foods every day, so don't overdo it, you can tolerate it.
I also really like a two yogurt that's filled with probiotics for the gut.
So those probiotic rich foods are high in enzymes, but they're also high in probiotics, which is good bacteria for your gut.
Adding in good bacteria can help alleviate digestive symptoms, and you don't necessarily have to take a probiotic supplement to do that. Now, let's talk fiber rich foods.
You want to include a lot of fiber, so that it feeds the good bacteria in your gut and it keeps things moving.
Stagnation in the gut breeds bloating, gas and constipation.
You kill two birds with one stone with kiwis. Both a high enzyme food and also a high fiber food.
Some other high fiber foods that are easy to digest and generally well tolerated are sweet potatoes, oats, brown rice and quinoa.
We have our gastric juice promoting foods.
The more you can increase gastric juice production, the better your digestion is going to be and the less bloating you're going to have.
This is going to be apple cider vinegar, bitter foods like kale, arugula, dandelion.
And know, you don't have to eat a whole salad of these things, but just chewing on them a little bit before you eat a meal is going to be super helpful.
And lastly, we have our anti-inflammatory foods.
These are foods that actually soothe and repair the lining of the gut.
Bone broth is my number one.
You can get bone broth powders and drink them.
Uh, I know Costco has one, Just Ingredients has one that I drink every single morning.
I think it's delicious.
Make your own bone broth using a chicken carcass.
Anytime I make, like, a whole chicken or I buy a rotisserie chicken, I will make bone broth with that.
I also buy cartons of bone broth at Trader Joe's or Walmart.
Ginger, fennel and peppermint are my other favorite foods that actually help soothe and stop bloating.
If you're actively bloated.
Those are foods I love to turn to.
You can drink these as teas, ginger you can obviously cook with,
and fennel is great in like casseroles or soups, but you can get any of them in tea form as well.
Here's the full list of everything that I talked about if you want to screenshot it for later.
